1. Spring AI Alibaba — Keep the Shell After a Pause

The problem

An AI agent can run shell commands. It keeps one shell open, so a command like cd build still applies to the next command.

Some steps need a person to approve them. The agent pauses, the person approves, and the agent continues. When it continued, it had lost track of its shell, so the next command failed with a NullPointerException.

What I changed

Each conversation has an id (threadId) that survives the pause. I added a small lookup table from that id to the open shell. When the agent resumes, it looks up its shell by id and keeps using it, still in the same folder.

sequenceDiagram autonumber actor Person participant Agent participant Table as Lookup table participant Shell Agent->>Shell: open a shell Agent->>Table: save shell under this conversation's id Agent->>Shell: cd build Agent-->>Person: pause, approval needed Person-->>Agent: approve, continue Agent->>Table: find the shell by id Table-->>Agent: same shell as before Agent->>Shell: make, still in the build folder Agent->>Table: remove the entry when finished Agent->>Shell: close the shell
  • The entry is removed when the conversation ends, so the table only holds shells that are still in use.
  • If a caller has no conversation id, the code raises a clear error instead of opening a shell nobody would close.
  • Eight unit tests cover saving, finding, removing, and keeping two conversations apart.

2. Google LangExtract — Retry Only the Piece That Failed

The problem

LangExtract splits a long document into pieces and sends them to Gemini at the same time. If Gemini briefly answered "busy" (503) or "too many requests" (429) for one piece, the whole document failed, and all the pieces that had already succeeded were thrown away.

What I changed

Each piece now retries on its own when the error is temporary. It waits about 1 second, then 2, then 4, up to a limit, and gives up after a few tries. Errors that retrying cannot fix are reported straight away.

flowchart LR Send["Send one piece
to Gemini"] OK{"Success?"} Done["Keep the result"] Temp{"Temporary error
and tries left?"} Wait["Wait, then
double the wait"] Fail["Report the error"] Send --> OK OK -- Yes --> Done OK -- No --> Temp Temp -- Yes --> Wait Wait --> Send Temp -- No --> Fail
Setting Default Meaning
max_retries3Extra tries per piece
retry_delay1 sFirst wait; doubles each time
max_retry_delay16 sLongest wait

Before merging, the maintainer built on my change: random variation in the waits so pieces do not all retry at the same moment, and a check that stops these retries from stacking on top of the Gemini SDK's own retries.

3. Kubernetes Java Client — A Tested Example for Patching

The problem

To change part of a Kubernetes object you send a PATCH request, and the request must say which patch format its body uses. With the generated Java client it is easy to send a patch for a custom resource without that format, and the server then rejects it. The library has a helper, PatchUtils, that sets it correctly, but there was no example for custom resources.

What I changed

  • A runnable example, PatchCustomObjectExample, that patches a custom resource from a JSON file.
  • A short README section: use PatchUtils for patches.
  • Tests against a mock server that check the exact request that goes out, for two patch formats, so the example cannot quietly stop working.
Object result =
    PatchUtils.patch(
        Object.class,
        () ->
            api.patchNamespacedCustomObject(
                    group, version, namespace, plural, name, new V1Patch(patchJson))
                .buildCall(null),
        V1Patch.PATCH_FORMAT_JSON_PATCH,
        client);

What These Have in Common

  • Keep changes focused. Repair lifecycle and integration boundaries without unrelated refactoring.
  • Make behavior verifiable. Add regression tests or isolate concurrency tests, with the scope documented in each PR.
  • Upstream evidence. Every linked contribution is merged; the PR pages retain the review and implementation history.
